about: The one record of how Common Shade's knowledge has changed, for /growing/ ('Watch Common Shade grow'), llms-full.txt and the exit card. One entry per change, reviewed by hand; tools/growth-candidates.js proposes candidates and never publishes. 'added' is the day the change reached the site (its merged pull request, 'pr'); 'event' is the date of the underlying work, as printed by its source or computed from its records ('span'). 'why' is Common Shade's reading; 'finding' is what a source says, quoted from text already on the site (the check confirms it appears there). 'links' join an entry to records on the map: basis 'record' when the connection is in the site's structured data, 'editorial' when it is our reviewed mapping. 'effort' names the check files behind the change; the page counts them into 'What it took to add this' and never types a number. Kinds, places, people and topics come from fixed lists (see tools/growth-text.js). IDs are stable.

entries.title: Heat right now: live readings for Asian cities
entries.why: A reading of today's heat, with a forecast, puts the rest of the site in the present tense. It helps a reader connect what the evidence says to the heat outside.
entries.review: Live data from Open-Meteo and data.gov.sg; readings are not checked by hand

links.why: Live readings and forecasts are where early action starts.

entries.title: What each vicious cycle costs, with Southeast Asian figures
entries.why: A cycle is easier to act on once its cost is visible. Each cost carries its own source, so a reader can check the figure before using it.
entries.review: Each figure links to its source
action: Read the costs of each cycle

links.why: The costs follow the cycles on the map, one by one.

entries.title: A week in the heat: one worker's money through a heatwave
entries.why: Following one illustrative household day by day shows how lost hours, medical bills and debt add up. It is a drawn example built from sourced figures, not one person's story.
entries.review: Illustrative; each figure links to its source

links.why: The week shows where a payout on a hot day could change the outcome.

entries.title: Paying for protection: routes, triggers, basis risk and cases
entries.why: Money that arrives before or during heat works differently from money after it. This guide sets out how each route pays, and where payouts can miss the people they were meant for.
entries.review: Each case links to its source

links.why: Risk pools are one of the routes the guide compares.
Heat-triggered payouts are explained with their basis risk.

entries.title: Plan a response: a step-by-step workbook, with additions from MCR2030
entries.why: A team can move from what the evidence says to a plan for its own place, step by step, in a workshop or alone. Its answers stay in the reader's browser.
entries.review: Each step links to its guidance

links.why: The workbook walks through what a heat action plan covers.

entries.title: A solutions library and country snapshots, from the October 2026 research
entries.why: Practical measures sit next to the places that use them, so a reader can see what exists before deciding what to try.
entries.review: Every link checked; unreachable links left out

effort.asked: What practical measures against heat exist across South and Southeast Asia, and where?
effort.open: Many measures have no published evaluation yet; the library says so where that is the case.

links.why: Cooling by design is among the measures the library documents.

entries.title: Solutions joined to the vicious cycle each one could break
entries.why: A measure means more when you can see which cycle it interrupts. Each link here is a reviewed mapping, not a measured effect.
entries.review: Editorial mapping, reviewed

links.why: Measures such as protecting households from disconnection in a heatwave are mapped to the energy poverty cycle.

entries.title: The heat network: who holds the need, who supplies, who connects
entries.why: Seeing organisations as demand, supply or platform shows where a partner could come from, and where nobody yet connects the two.

event.what: Organisations described from their own pages

entries.review: Each organisation links to its own page; listing is not endorsement

links.why: Each organisation record names the actions it works on.

entries.title: How heat is reported: a bibliography of coverage in many languages
entries.why: Coverage shapes what decision-makers notice. Reading it together shows which harms and places get attention and which stay quiet, without judging any outlet.
entries.review: Every link checked; journalist names removed; unverified links held back

links.why: Harms that coverage misses are part of the cycle that keeps heat invisible.

entries.title: Correction: the site stopped telling people what to do
entries.why: The people closest to the heat know their places best. Describing what helps, and what it depends on, keeps the site a place to learn alongside them.

finding.text: Many pages spoke in an instructing voice, telling cities, employers, funders and others what to do.

entries.review: Published on /corrections/, with an apology; a check keeps it from returning

links.why: Every correction is listed with what changed and why.

entries.title: Describing what we could see, never what someone did not do
entries.why: A gap in a record is not proof that nothing happened. The site now says what it could find and where it looked, so an absence reads as a question rather than a judgement.
entries.review: Editorial revision, enforced by the voice check

links.why: The approach page explains how the site words what it cannot confirm.

entries.title: A learning agenda: the questions the evidence has not yet answered
entries.why: Naming what nobody knows yet is as useful as summarising what is known. Each question sits beside the cycle it belongs to, with a study that could answer it.

event.what: Questions drawn from the limits studies state

entries.review: Each question restates limits its cited studies give themselves; designs are our suggestions

links.why: One question asks how much of the load on clinics in a heatwave is heat illness.

entries.title: Paying when heat strikes: insurance, pools, credit and forecast funds
entries.why: Whether a payout arrived, and when, matters more than whether a product exists. This section follows what is documented about each instrument paying out.
entries.review: Every link checked and archived

effort.asked: Which financial instruments pay out when heat strikes in Asia, and is there a record that they did?
effort.open: For many instruments, no public record yet shows a payout reaching people.

links.why: Forecast-based funds are one of the instruments followed.

entries.why: The first month run through every check showed the pipeline can hold back what it cannot confirm. Records that only a secondary report described stayed held.

finding.text: Nearly 600 scientists, business leaders, philanthropists and health experts met in Bangkok from 6 to 9 October 2026.

entries.review: Every source checked against its own text; unconfirmed records held

effort.asked: What changed for heat protection in South and Southeast Asia in October 2026?
effort.open: How heat-health pilots keep their footing once funding ends.

action: Read the State of the field

links.why: Bangladesh's first urban heatwave action plan joins the plans on the Atlas.

entries.title: Question opened: how do heat-health pilots keep their footing once funding ends?
entries.why: Protection that stops when a grant stops leaves people exposed again. Asking the question openly invites the people who have seen it happen to share what worked.

event.what: Raised by a funder's own account of the region

entries.review: Knowledge-base question record, checked with its source

links.why: Lasting budgets are one answer the question points towards.

entries.title: Atlas of Asia's heat: heatwaves since 1998 and the plans that followed
entries.why: Placing heatwaves and the plans that came after them on one map shows how protection has followed experience, place by place.

entries.review: Each heatwave and milestone links to its source

entries.title: India heat action plan archive: verified plans and guidance from across India
entries.why: Plans are easier to learn from side by side. Each one is verified, typed and dated as printed, so a city can find a neighbour's plan and see how it changed.

effort.open: Unverified leads remain, and plan scoring against the rubric is planned.

entries.title: Heat and the health of mothers, children and minds
entries.why: Pregnancy, newborn health, mental health and gender-based violence were thin on the map. Adding them, with an evidence brief, makes these harms visible next to the better-known ones.
entries.review: Sources checked, with Europe PMC for publisher pages that block automated reading

effort.asked: What does the evidence say about heat and maternal, newborn, child and mental health in the region?
effort.open: The learning agenda carries the questions this evidence leaves open.

links.why: The new evidence sits under the lever for protecting pregnancy and newborns.
Mothers and newborns are one of the groups the map now separates.

entries.title: A weekly evidence review, signed off by a person
entries.why: New studies arrive every week. A Monday harvest opens a review, and only studies a person accepts join their cycles, so the map grows without lowering its bar.
entries.review: Each study accepted by a person before it joins the map

links.why: Accepted studies join their cycles on the evidence map.

entries.title: India's Heat Resilient Cities Framework (2026), across the site
entries.why: The framework moves cities from emergency response towards lasting change, with the people most exposed at the centre. It now informs the glossary, the planning checklist and the cities it names.

finding.text: A city that moves beyond emergency response each hot season towards lasting change in its buildings, water, transport, work, health services and cooling, with the people most exposed to heat at the centre.

entries.review: Cited from the publisher's own page

links.why: The framework extends what a heat action plan covers.

entries.title: Every harm paired with hope: the nearest places to act, or an honest gap
entries.why: A harm without a way forward can leave a reader stuck. Each harm now points to the actions closest to it, or says plainly that none is documented yet.
entries.review: Built from the map's own links between harms and actions

links.why: The pairing uses the links already on the map.

entries.title: How heat became visible: a graded timeline of when the world began to notice
entries.why: Knowing when science, health, labour, finance and the UN each noticed heat shows who was still missing. Each event carries a grade, so certainty is never overstated.
entries.review: Every source checked; uncertain events graded, unconfirmed ones dropped and listed

effort.asked: When did science, health, labour, finance and the UN begin to notice extreme heat, and who was still missing?
effort.open: Several early events stay graded uncertain because their sources could not be read.

links.why: The timeline traces how heat moved out of the cycle that kept it invisible.

entries.title: Correction: what cooling centres and fans can and cannot do
entries.why: Readers plan real protection from these pages. Saying what the evidence supports, and what it depends on, keeps a plan from resting on more than the evidence holds.

finding.text: Two actions said more than the evidence shows: that public cooling spaces and check-ins save lives in every heatwave, and that efficient fans put safe cooling within reach of every household.

entries.review: Published on /corrections/, with an apology

links.why: The cooling centres action now says what its benefit depends on.
The affordable cooling action now matches cooling to the local heat.

entries.title: Lenses on what the map was missing

entries.title: Watch for: documented side effects of actions that otherwise help
entries.why: An action can help one group and burden another. Showing documented side effects next to each action is a revised reading of what helps, not a reason to stop.

links.why: Most roof treatments lowered indoor heat in one study, but one coating left rooms hotter; the action now says so.
Watering fields can raise the humid heat farmworkers feel; the action now carries that watch-out.
